subject: Literature
title: Prescribed African and Non-African Prose
outline: African Prose: Adimora-Ezeigbo, So the Path Does Not Die
Plot, structure, characterisation and themes of the African novel
Non-African Prose: Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird
Plot by parts, Maycomb society, the Tom Robinson trial
Narrative technique, symbolism and point of view in both novels
Comparative themes: prejudice, courage, tradition and moral growth

modules.title: Module 1: So the Path Does Not Die (Akachi Adimora-Ezeigbo) - Africa
modules.html:
1.1 The Author and Context

Professor Akachi Adimora-Ezeigbo is a Nigerian novelist, critic and scholar, and a leading voice of the third generation of Nigerian women writers. Her theory of snail-sense feminism proposes that the African woman should negotiate patriarchal terrain with the tact, patience and resilience of a snail crossing rough ground — neither surrendering nor colliding head-on. So the Path Does Not Die (2010) applies this outlook to the question of harmful traditional practices, particularly female genital mutilation, and to the survival of a woman's dignity across village, city and diaspora.

1.2 Plot Overview

The novel follows Ejiaka, born into the community of Aludo, whose mother, Nneka, resists the ritual circumcision of her daughter and pays a social price for that refusal. Ejiaka grows up marked as different, an 'uncircumcised' girl in a community where the rite is the passport to womanhood and marriage. The narrative traces her progress through:

  1. Childhood in Aludo – the closeness of mother and daughter, the pressure of the umuada and elders, ostracism and taunts, the death and loss that harden Ejiaka's resolve.
  2. Education and self-making – schooling, the discovery of books, mentors and friendship, movement to the city, and the growth of a professional identity.
  3. Love, rejection and marriage – relationships complicated by the stigma attached to her body and by family expectation.
  4. Travel abroad and return – exposure to other worlds broadens Ejiaka's perspective without severing her from home; the title's 'path' is the continuity of the community that must be kept alive but also cleared of thorns.
  5. Advocacy and reconciliation – Ejiaka commits herself to the campaign against female genital mutilation and to the empowerment of girls, working within the community rather than against it, in the snail-sense manner.

1.3 Characterisation

  • Ejiaka – protagonist; intelligent, resilient, wounded but not embittered; her growth from stigmatised child to confident advocate structures the novel as a female Bildungsroman.
  • Nneka – the mother whose courageous refusal begins the conflict; she embodies maternal love as moral courage.
  • The elders and the umuada – guardians of custom, not simply villains: they express the community's genuine fear that abandoning the rite will destroy identity.
  • Friends, teachers and mentors – agents of enlightenment who show that education is the strongest instrument of change.
  • Male figures – range from the supportive to the deeply conservative, illustrating that patriarchy is sustained by consent as well as by force.

1.4 Themes

  1. Harmful traditional practices and the female body – the central concern.
  2. Tradition versus modernity – not a simple rejection of culture but a call to prune it.
  3. Education as liberation.
  4. Motherhood, sisterhood and female solidarity.
  5. Stigma, ostracism and endurance.
  6. Migration, exile and return.
  7. Continuity: 'so the path does not die' — the survival of the community through its children.

1.5 Style

Realistic third-person narration with strong access to Ejiaka's inner life; Igbo proverbs, songs and idioms transliterated into English; symbolic titles and chapter movement from village to city to abroad; a documentary strain in the advocacy sections; and a hopeful, forward-looking close typical of reformist fiction.

examples.q: Explain the significance of the novel's title, So the Path Does Not Die.
examples.a: The 'path' is a multiple symbol. Literally it is the bush path linking homesteads in Aludo, a path that dies when it is no longer walked. Communally it is the lineage: an Igbo proverb holds that a family line must produce children so that the path to the compound does not become overgrown, so the title invokes continuity, memory and belonging. Ironically, however, the practice defended in the name of continuity — female circumcision — is itself shown to endanger life and fertility, and thus to threaten the very path it claims to preserve. Adimora-Ezeigbo therefore uses the title to reframe the debate: reformers like Nneka and Ejiaka are not enemies of tradition but its true custodians, since only by removing what maims its daughters can the community survive. The title finally extends to knowledge and advocacy: the path is kept alive when one generation clears it for the next.

examples.q: Discuss Nneka as a foil to the community elders.
examples.a: Nneka's refusal to have Ejiaka circumcised sets the novel's conflict in motion, and her character gains definition by contrast with the elders and the umuada. Where they act from collective authority, she acts from individual conviction; where they invoke ancestral precedent, she invokes her child's health and future; where they can absorb dissent by ostracism, she must bear that ostracism alone. Yet the contrast is not crude. The elders are given a coherent case — the fear that a community which abandons its rites will lose its identity and its daughters will be unmarriageable — and Nneka herself never repudiates Igbo culture: she continues to live within it, observing its other norms. This is snail-sense resistance: patient, embedded, tactical. As a foil, therefore, Nneka does not merely oppose the elders; she exposes the difference between custom as living wisdom and custom as unexamined habit.

modules.title: Module 2: To Kill a Mockingbird (Harper Lee) - Non-Africa
modules.html:
2.1 Context

Harper Lee (1926–2016) published To Kill a Mockingbird in 1960, at the height of the American Civil Rights Movement. It is set in the fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama, during the Great Depression, roughly 1933–1935. Racial segregation under the Jim Crow laws was legally enforced; an all-white jury, a black defendant and a white accuser made acquittal almost impossible. The novel is narrated in retrospect by Jean Louise 'Scout' Finch, recalling her childhood from adulthood.

2.2 Plot

SectionMain Events
Part One (Chs 1–11)Scout, her brother Jem and their friend Dill spend summers obsessed with the reclusive Arthur 'Boo' Radley. Gifts appear in a knot-hole; Nathan Radley cements it up. Scout's difficulties at school; Atticus's lessons in empathy ('you never really understand a person until you climb into his skin and walk around in it'). Atticus shoots the mad dog Tim Johnson, revealing hidden skill. Mrs Dubose's morphine withdrawal teaches Jem 'real courage'. Atticus accepts the defence of Tom Robinson.
Part Two (Chs 12–21)Calpurnia takes the children to First Purchase church. Aunt Alexandra arrives to instil family pride. A lynch mob at the jail is dispersed when Scout innocently speaks to Mr Cunningham. The trial: Bob Ewell and Mayella Ewell accuse Tom Robinson of rape; Atticus proves the injuries were inflicted by a left-handed man while Tom's left arm is crippled, and suggests Mayella made advances to Tom and was beaten by her father. Despite the evidence the jury convicts.
Part Two (Chs 22–31)Tom is shot dead attempting to escape prison. Bob Ewell, humiliated, spits at Atticus, threatens the judge and Tom's widow, and finally attacks Jem and Scout on the way home from the Halloween pageant. Boo Radley saves them, killing Ewell. Sheriff Heck Tate records the death as a fall on his own knife, to spare Boo publicity. Scout, standing on the Radley porch, at last sees the street from Boo's point of view.

2.3 Characters

  • Scout – narrator; tomboyish, quick-tempered, questioning; her double perspective (child experiencing / adult recalling) allows both innocence and irony.
  • Atticus Finch – lawyer and moral centre; defends Tom knowing he will lose, because 'before I can live with other folks I've got to live with myself'.
  • Jem – older brother whose faith in justice is broken by the verdict; his growth is the novel's tragedy of disillusion.
  • Tom Robinson – honest, generous black labourer destroyed by prejudice; a 'mockingbird'.
  • Boo (Arthur) Radley – the feared recluse who is finally the children's protector; the second 'mockingbird'.
  • Bob Ewell – ignorant, vindictive, abusive; villain of the piece.
  • Mayella Ewell – both victim and perjurer; her loneliness and abuse complicate blame.
  • Calpurnia – black housekeeper bridging two worlds; educator of the children.
  • Miss Maudie, Heck Tate, Judge Taylor, Dolphus Raymond – figures of quiet decency who show Maycomb is not uniformly bigoted.

2.4 Themes and Symbols

  1. Racial injustice and the failure of the law.
  2. Innocence and its destruction – the mockingbird symbol: 'it's a sin to kill a mockingbird', a bird that only makes music.
  3. Moral education and empathy – the skin-walking lesson framing the novel.
  4. Courage – defined not as 'a man with a gun in his hand' but as persistence when defeat is certain.
  5. Class and social hierarchy – Finches, Cunninghams, Ewells and black Maycomb.
  6. Gender expectations – the pressure on Scout to be a 'lady'.
  7. Appearance versus reality – Boo the monster becomes Boo the saviour.

Other symbols: the mad dog (rabid racism that Atticus must shoot down); the knot-hole gifts (attempted friendship); the camellias (forgiveness after anger); the snowman of mixed mud and snow (racial mixture); the Halloween ham costume (which saves Scout's life).

2.5 Narrative Technique

Retrospective first-person narration produces a controlled double vision: the child reports without fully understanding, while the adult voice supplies irony and moral weight. The Bildungsroman structure moves from play to trial to violence. The first-person limitation is also a device of suspense — because Scout cannot see inside the Radley house or the jury room, the reader shares her exclusion. Regional dialect, humour and small-town gossip give texture, while the trial section adopts an almost documentary rhythm of question and answer.

examples.q: Explain the mockingbird symbol and identify the characters it applies to.
examples.a: Atticus tells the children they may shoot bluejays but that 'it's a sin to kill a mockingbird', and Miss Maudie explains why: mockingbirds do not eat gardens or nest in corncribs; they do nothing but sing for people's enjoyment. The bird therefore symbolises harmless innocence, and killing it symbolises the destruction of the defenceless by the powerful. Tom Robinson is the clearest mockingbird: he helped Mayella out of pity, asked no payment, and is destroyed first by perjury and a prejudiced jury and then by seventeen bullets in a prison yard. Boo Radley is the second: shut away and turned into a neighbourhood monster by rumour, he leaves gifts, mends Jem's trousers, covers Scout with a blanket and finally saves both children; dragging him into the publicity of a trial, Scout says, would be 'sort of like shootin' a mockingbird'. Arguably Mayella Ewell and even Jem's shattered faith belong to the same pattern of innocence damaged by a corrupt social order.

examples.q: How does Atticus dismantle the prosecution case at the trial, and why does he still lose?
examples.a: Atticus establishes three decisive facts. First, no doctor was ever called, so there is no medical evidence of rape. Second, Mayella's injuries were concentrated on the right side of her face, consistent with a blow from a left-handed assailant; he demonstrates in court that Bob Ewell is left-handed, whereas Tom Robinson's left arm was crippled in a cotton-gin accident and is twelve inches shorter and useless, making him incapable of inflicting those injuries or of holding a struggling woman down. Third, he elicits from Mayella herself a picture of isolation and abuse at home and suggests that she kissed Tom, was caught by her father, and accused Tom to bury her shame. Tom's fatal error is honesty: he says he felt 'sorry for her', an unbearable presumption for a black man in Maycomb. Atticus loses because the verdict is not decided by evidence but by the racial code of the community: in the words of the novel, in Maycomb's courts a white man's word beats a black man's every time. Judge Taylor's appointment of Atticus, the length of the jury's deliberation, and a Cunningham's reported hesitation nevertheless register the first small crack in that code.

quiz.q: So the Path Does Not Die was written by
quiz.solution: Professor Akachi Adimora-Ezeigbo, a Nigerian novelist and critic, wrote the novel, published in 2010.

quiz.q: The central social issue confronted in So the Path Does Not Die is
options: female genital mutilation and the stigma attached to resisting it
quiz.solution: The novel centres on the refusal of circumcision for Ejiaka and the consequences of that refusal for mother and daughter.

quiz.q: The protagonist of So the Path Does Not Die is
quiz.solution: Ejiaka is the girl whose growth from stigmatised child to advocate structures the novel.

quiz.q: Adimora-Ezeigbo's feminist theory is known as
quiz.solution: Snail-sense feminism advocates patient, tactful negotiation with patriarchy rather than direct confrontation.

quiz.q: The 'path' in the novel's title symbolises chiefly
quiz.solution: The path stands for the survival of the community and its lineage, which the novel argues is best preserved by removing harmful practices.

quiz.q: To Kill a Mockingbird is set in
quiz.solution: The fictional town of Maycomb in Alabama during the Great Depression is the novel's setting.

quiz.q: The narrator of To Kill a Mockingbird is
quiz.solution: Scout narrates retrospectively as an adult recalling her childhood, giving a double perspective.

quiz.q: Tom Robinson is accused of
quiz.solution: Bob and Mayella Ewell accuse Tom of raping her, though the evidence points to Bob Ewell's own violence.

quiz.q: Atticus proves that Mayella's attacker was
quiz.solution: The injuries to the right side of her face indicate a left-handed assailant; Bob Ewell is left-handed while Tom's left arm is crippled.

quiz.q: Which character is described as a 'mockingbird' for being harmless yet destroyed?
quiz.solution: Tom sings, so to speak, only for others' good: he helped Mayella without payment and is destroyed by prejudice.

quiz.q: Boo Radley finally emerges from his house to
options: save Jem and Scout from Bob Ewell
quiz.solution: Boo kills Bob Ewell during the Halloween attack and carries the injured Jem home.

quiz.q: Mrs Dubose's struggle teaches Jem that real courage is
options: a man with a gun in his hand
knowing you are licked before you begin but seeing it through
quiz.solution: Atticus praises her fight to die free of morphine addiction as courage: persisting when defeat is certain.

quiz.q: Calpurnia's importance in the novel lies in her role as
options: a bridge between the white and black communities
quiz.solution: As housekeeper and surrogate mother who also takes the children to First Purchase church, Calpurnia links the two Maycombs.

quiz.q: The mad dog Tim Johnson is generally read as a symbol of
options: the madness of racism that Atticus must confront
quiz.solution: Atticus, the reluctant marksman, shoots down a rabid animal threatening the street, as he later confronts the sickness of racial prejudice.

quiz.q: Sheriff Heck Tate insists Bob Ewell fell on his own knife in order to
options: shield the reclusive Boo Radley from publicity
quiz.solution: Dragging the shy Boo into the limelight would, in Scout's words, be like shooting a mockingbird.

quiz.q: Atticus's central lesson to Scout is that you never understand a person until you
options: climb into his skin and walk around in it
quiz.solution: This lesson in empathy frames the novel and is fulfilled when Scout stands on the Radley porch and sees the street from Boo's viewpoint.

quiz.q: Tom Robinson's fatal admission during the trial is that he
options: could not use his left hand
quiz.solution: For a black man in 1930s Alabama to pity a white woman was an intolerable claim to superiority, and it turned the jury against him.

quiz.q: Both So the Path Does Not Die and To Kill a Mockingbird explore
options: prejudice and the courage required to resist it
quiz.solution: One examines gendered and traditional prejudice in an Igbo community; the other racial prejudice in the American South. Both celebrate individuals who resist at personal cost.

quiz.q: Aunt Alexandra comes to the Finch household mainly to
options: give Scout a feminine influence and instil family pride
quiz.solution: She believes Scout needs a lady's upbringing and that the children must be taught the importance of the Finch name.

quiz.q: Education in So the Path Does Not Die functions chiefly as
options: a means of leaving Africa permanently
an instrument of liberation and advocacy
a mark of social class only
quiz.solution: Schooling gives Ejiaka the language, confidence and platform to campaign for change within her community rather than to abandon it.
